bull.b: Record IET bookings, a 2.2x book-to-bill ratio, and record RPO provide substantial multi-year revenue visibility. This backlog supports planning, utilization, and recurring service opportunities, helping Baker Hughes sustain growth even when near-term customer spending fluctuates.

Strong operating cash flow and free cash flow give Baker Hughes internal funding capacity for investment, debt reduction, and shareholder returns. Combined with expanding EBITDA margins, this indicates improved operating execution and a stronger earnings base over the next several quarters.

The Chart acquisition expands Baker Hughes beyond traditional oilfield exposure into cryogenic storage, heat exchangers, carbon capture, and industrial aftermarket services. Its identified cost and cross-selling synergies could diversify revenue and support structurally higher margins.

bear.b: The sharp increase in debt relative to equity reduces financial flexibility and raises sensitivity to cyclical energy markets. Although management plans to deleverage, elevated leverage can constrain capital allocation and increase the consequences of weaker operating conditions during the next several quarters.

The sharply negative TTM revenue trend creates uncertainty about the durability and timing of Baker Hughes’ growth. Steady gross margins and improved profitability are encouraging, but inconsistent top-line performance can limit operating leverage and make forward earnings more dependent on project timing.

Large IET orders strengthen long-term visibility but do not guarantee near-term revenue growth when conversion stretches beyond 2027. Longer GTE cycles and supply-chain timing can defer cash generation, leave quarterly results uneven, and require sustained execution before backlog becomes reported sales.
